                                                           Agentic Infrastructure | Comments in Project No. 58481




              BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS
                      PROJECT NO. 58481
RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS
                     UNDER PURA § 37.0561

                  COMMENTS OF AGENTIC INFRASTRUCTURE

                                                                                                 April 16, 2026
To the Public Utility Commission of Texas:

STATEMENT OF INTEREST
Agentic Infrastructure (“Agentic”) appreciates the opportunity to comment in Project No. 58481
regarding the standards that will govern large-load interconnection in ERCOT under PURA §
37.0561. Agentic is a Texas-focused powered-land development platform that sites, designs,
structures, and executes speed-to-power solutions for AI and digital infrastructure. Agentic is
currently developing 7.25 GW of large load across four properties, supported by 8.25 GW of
generation resources currently in the ERCOT interconnection queue, with additional sites under
development. Because Agentic develops large-load campuses using load flexibility and co-
located storage and generation, it has a direct interest in a framework that maximizes economic
development, minimizes stranded-cost risk, and maintains reliability.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
These comments make five principal points:
 • Batch Zero should not adopt the distortions created by the legacy firm-service study process.
    In congested territories, especially around major load centers, project advancement has
    depended in material part on how and when individual TSPs elect to advance studies rather
    than on where load most rationally prefers to site.
 • A studied-project screen that relies too heavily on legacy study advancement will
    overrepresent remote and radial projects and underrepresent financeable, durable projects
    near major load centers, increasing the risk of inefficient transmission expansion and
    stranded costs.
 • Projects that elect to be studied as Controllable Load Resources (“CLRs”) or with sufficient
    self-supplied generation or storage (“BYOG”) should be eligible for Batch Zero studied
    treatment if they execute the intermediate agreement and satisfy the required financial-
    security obligations.
 • Significant financial security at the intermediate-agreement stage is an appropriate mechanism
    for screening speculative projects. Direct transmission cost allocation, however, should not
    become the primary gating device for whether commercially actionable projects can
    advance.




                                      Project No. 58481 | Page 1
                                                              Agentic Infrastructure | Comments in Project No. 58481




 • Coordination with related proceedings - particularly Project Nos. 59142 and 58484 - can
    reinforce a TSP-agnostic framework that better aligns private incentives with public
    planning goals while preserving reliability.

INTRODUCTION
Texas has become the nation’s most attractive market for large-scale AI and digital infrastructure
because it combines abundant energy resources, available land, a pro-growth policy
environment, and ERCOT’s market design. That success has also created the most important
transmission-planning challenge in ERCOT’s history. As of April 2026, ERCOT reported more
than 400 GW of large-load requests in the interconnection queue. The question is no longer
whether large load will continue to seek entry into ERCOT; the question is whether the standards
adopted now will produce a transmission expansion path that is efficient, durable, and fair to
existing consumers.
The Commission’s work in Project No. 58481 is therefore foundational. If the rules adopted here
allow Batch Zero to be shaped by the procedural bottlenecks of the legacy firm-service study
process, the resulting study set will not accurately reflect where load actually wants to locate. By
contrast, if the Commission allows financially committed projects that can privately manage
interim transmission risk to be studied on a rational basis, the Batch Zero process can produce a
materially better statewide planning outcome.

I. BATCH ZERO SHOULD NOT IMPORT THE DISTORTIONS CREATED BY THE
LEGACY FIRM-SERVICE STUDY PROCESS.
The current draft inclusion criteria for base and studied load risk converting the outcomes of the
legacy process into the input assumptions for Batch Zero. That would be a structural mistake. In
high-interest areas, the sequential firm-service study process and TSP-specific advancement
decisions have materially affected which projects reach study milestones. Those procedural
outcomes are not a neutral proxy for long-term system value, financeability, or where load most
efficiently prefers to site.

A. Large AI loads naturally prefer major load centers because those locations are more
financeable, readily operable, and reliably connected to the broader grid.
Unlike traditional heavy industrial projects that may need to locate near a mine mouth, a process
feedstock, or in regions with relaxed emissions standards, hyperscale data centers
disproportionately value proximity to labor, fiber, public resources, and transportation
infrastructure. For those reasons, load-center siting usually best aligns private incentives with the
public interest.

B. The legacy study process creates a self-reinforcing feedback loop that pushes projects
away from their preferred locations.
The problem can be stated as follows:



                                        Project No. 58481 | Page 2
                                                                  Agentic Infrastructure | Comments in Project No. 58481




 1. Developers request service in the locations that best minimize total cost of service for the
    ultimate end use.
 2. Legacy firm-service planning studies upgrades sequentially and advances projects unevenly
    across territories, especially where the RPG process has become deadlocked.
 3. Projects in the highest-interest load-center territories can remain unadvanced for long periods
    even after substantial commercial progress has been made.
 4. Remote portions of the grid therefore show a disproportionately large share of projects that
    are able to clear intermediate study milestones.
 5. Developers then pursue those remote locations, not because they are superior, but because
    they appear more likely to advance.
If Batch Zero uses those legacy advancement outcomes as a principal filter for studied treatment,
it will misread the market. The Commission should not let inherited bottlenecks determine which
projects shape the largest single phase of grid expansion in ERCOT history.




                           Figure 1. Large loads naturally prefer metro load centers.




   Figure 2. Under the legacy process, projects in load centers are more likely to remain unstudied even where
                                              demand is strongest.



                                            Project No. 58481 | Page 3
                                                                     Agentic Infrastructure | Comments in Project No. 58481




Figure 3. If Batch Zero eligibility tracks legacy study progress, the resulting project class is distorted toward remote
                                                       locations.

II. CURRENT STUDY PROGRESS AND EXISTING FIRM AWARDS SHOW LEGACY
PROCESSES ARE INEFFICNETLY EXPANDING TRANSMISSION
The available data already illustrates a distortion. As shown below, a significant share of the
projects that have completed or nearly completed studies are located in West Texas, while major
metro load-center territories continue to show substantial volumes of projects that have not been
studied. That pattern does not prove that remote projects are inherently superior. It shows that
procedural advancement decisions matter.




                                       Figure 4. Existing load request progress
                                    Source: ERCOT TAC presentation, Mar. 26, 2026.




                                               Project No. 58481 | Page 4
                                                               Agentic Infrastructure | Comments in Project No. 58481




                  Figure 5. Load requests approved, under review, and not studied by TSP
                              Source: ERCOT TAC presentation, Mar. 26, 2026.

The problem is compounded by the current utilization of awarded firm capacity. At TAC on
March 26, 2026, ERCOT presented data indicating that approved large loads were using far less
than their fully awarded firm transmission capacity on a coincident basis. When projects using a
fraction of awarded capacity are treated as if they consume the full award for planning purposes,
incremental studies become more constrained than the actual system experience suggests.




                         Figure 6. Approved large loads by zone and project type
                              Source: ERCOT TAC presentation, Mar. 26, 2026.




                                         Project No. 58481 | Page 5
                                                               Agentic Infrastructure | Comments in Project No. 58481




                          Figure 7. Observed use of approved large-load capacity
                               Source: ERCOT TAC presentation, Mar. 26, 2026.

A. Load-center projects generally deliver broader public value than remote or radial
projects.
When a large project sites near a major load center, the resulting network upgrades are more
likely to support multiple present and future users. Those locations also tend to offer:
 • better access to labor, transportation, fiber, water, and existing public infrastructure;
 • greater alternative-use value if the initial end use changes;
 • higher confidence that the project can be financed, built, and fully utilized; and
 • a stronger case that transmission investment will serve a broad class of consumers rather than
    a narrow radial pocket.
By contrast, projects in remote or radial locations more often present the opposite profile:
 • limited alternative use if the original hyperscale customer does not materialize;
 • weaker logistics for construction and operations;
 • fewer nearby beneficiaries for large network upgrades; and
 • greater stranded-cost risk if the project is delayed, downsized, or never reaches full operation.

III. PROJECTS THAT CAN PRIVATELY MANAGE INTERIM TRANSMISSION RISK
THROUGH CLR OR BYOG STRUCTURES SHOULD BE ELIGIBLE FOR BATCH
ZERO STUDIED TREATMENT.
The most practical way to correct the distortion without disadvantaging firm load is to allow
projects that can assume interim transmission risk privately to be studied in Batch Zero. A
project that elects CLR treatment or that proposes sufficient self-supplied generation or storage is

                                         Project No. 58481 | Page 6
                                                              Agentic Infrastructure | Comments in Project No. 58481




not asking the Commission to ignore reliability. It is offering a different risk allocation: the
project takes on interim transmission risk privately while ERCOT and the TSP preserve the
ability to study, plan, and condition service appropriately.
That approach produces better information for statewide planning, better siting incentives, and
greater confidence that the studied project set reflects commercially actionable projects rather
than only those projects lucky enough to advance through legacy bottlenecks.

A. Agentic recommends a clear and TSP-agnostic eligibility test for Batch Zero studied
treatment.
A project should be eligible for Batch Zero studied treatment if it satisfies all of the following
conditions:
 1. The project has an LLI number and an identified point of interconnection.
 2. The project executes the intermediate agreement and posts the financial security required
    under Project No. 58481.
 3. The project either (a) is included in the 2026 RTP, (b) elects to be studied as a Controllable
    Load Resource, or (c) elects to be studied with sufficient self-supplied generation and/or
    energy storage.
This framework would improve Batch Zero without changing the treatment of traditional firm
load. It would not compel any project to take CLR or BYOG treatment. It would simply allow
projects that are prepared to assume interim risk privately to be studied on a more rational basis.

B. A project that ultimately cannot satisfy its elected CLR or BYOG obligations should roll
to the next batch rather than distort the current one.
If a project qualifies for Batch Zero studied treatment by electing CLR or BYOG status but later
fails to demonstrate that it can satisfy those obligations at the time of the interconnection
agreement, the project should not retain the benefit of that election. It should move to Batch 1.
That safeguard preserves integrity while still allowing the Batch Zero study set to reflect projects
that are commercially real and operationally flexible.

IV. THE COMMISSION SHOULD USE FINANCIAL SECURITY TO SCREEN
SPECULATIVE PROJECTS WITHOUT RELYING ON DIRECT COST ALLOCATION
TO ADVANCE COMMERCIAL ACTIVITY
Agentic supports significant financial-security obligations at the intermediate-agreement stage.
Meaningful deposits are an effective screen against speculative or phantom projects and, to a
limited degree, can also reduce the risk that ratepayers fund network expansions for non-viable
loads.
At the same time, the Commission should avoid making direct transmission cost allocation a
principal component of the batch process. Direct cost allocation can stall commercially
actionable projects, create recursive re-study problems, and cause the feasible upgrade solution
to shift as projects fall out of the queue. A framework that allows willing projects to assume

                                        Project No. 58481 | Page 7
                                                             Agentic Infrastructure | Comments in Project No. 58481




interim transmission risk privately is more likely to accelerate real economic activity while
producing better long-run transmission outcomes.

A. Market-based siting incentives can reduce stranded-cost risk without centrally dictating
where load must locate.
Where private parties are allowed to manage interim risk, they naturally gravitate toward
locations where the total project economics are strongest. For hyperscale digital infrastructure,
that typically means locations near major load centers. Those same locations are also the places
where incremental transmission investment is most likely to provide durable socialized value.
This is why Agentic supports a framework that relies on readiness, financial commitment, and
private risk assumption, over utility-by-utility advancement discretion, to determine which
projects shape Batch Zero.

V. THE COMMISSION SHOULD ADOPT SPECIFIC REVISIONS IN PROJECT NO.
58481 AND COORDINATE THOSE REVISIONS WITH PROJECT NOS. 59142 AND
58484.
Agentic respectfully requests that the Commission incorporate the following principles into the
final 58481 framework:
 • Use the intermediate agreement and associated financial-security requirements as the
    principal filter for commercial seriousness.
 • Permit Batch Zero studied treatment for projects that elect CLR treatment or sufficient self-
    supplied generation or storage, provided they satisfy the recommended readiness criteria.
 • Ensure that Batch Zero studied eligibility does not depend on inconsistent legacy study-
    advancement practices across different TSP territories.
 • Require any project qualifying through CLR or BYOG status to demonstrate compliance with
    those obligations before executing the final interconnection agreement, or else move to the
    next batch.
 • Coordinate the 58481 framework with Project No. 59142 so that the batch-study rules adopt
    the same logic for studied eligibility.
 • Coordinate with Project No. 58484 to preserve market-based cost signals, including a non-
    coincident peak charge for large loads and other improvements that better align
    responsibility with actual system use. Agentic further supports the proposals advanced in
    Project No. 58484 to improve the fairness and efficacy of transmission cost-management
    programs. Those reforms would reinforce the market signals needed to discourage inefficient
    siting and better align private behavior with system costs.

CONCLUSION
Texas has a singular opportunity to channel unprecedented large-load demand into a
transmission-expansion path that strengthens reliability and broadens economic development


                                       Project No. 58481 | Page 8
                                                            Agentic Infrastructure | Comments in Project No. 58481




without saddling existing consumers with unnecessary stranded-cost or excess transmission risk.
Project No. 58481, 59142, and 58484 can either perpetuate the distortions of the legacy process
or correct them. The Commission should choose the latter.
For the reasons set out above, Agentic respectfully requests that the Commission adopt a TSP-
agnostic framework that (i) screens speculative projects through meaningful financial-security
requirements, (ii) allows CLR and BYOG projects that can privately manage interim
transmission risk to qualify for Batch Zero studied treatment, and (iii) preserves market
incentives to site where transmission investment is most likely to produce durable public value.

Respectfully submitted,
AGENTIC INFRASTRUCTURE LLC

                             Standalone Executive Summary
These comments support a Project No. 58481 framework that filters out speculative large-load
projects through meaningful intermediate-agreement commitments and financial security, while
avoiding a Batch Zero study set distorted by legacy study bottlenecks.
 • Batch Zero should not be defined primarily by which projects advanced farthest under the
    legacy firm-service process, because that process reflects uneven TSP study timing rather
    than true statewide load-siting preferences.
 • A distorted Batch Zero dataset would overweight remote or radial projects, increase stranded-
    cost exposure, and understate the extent to which credible large load would prefer to site
    near major Texas load centers.
 • Projects that execute the intermediate agreement, satisfy required financial security, and
    demonstrate real commercial progress should be eligible for studied treatment when they are
    included in the 2026 RTP, elect CLR treatment, or elect study treatment with sufficient self-
    supplied generation or storage.
 • A CLR/BYOG pathway improves both private and public outcomes by allowing willing
    developers to manage interim transmission risk privately, improving financeability,
    supporting more efficient load-center siting, and producing transmission upgrades with
    broader socialized value.
 • Project No. 58481 should therefore be coordinated with the related Batch Zero (59142) and
    transmission-cost (58484) proceedings so that the Commission adopts a coherent framework
    that maximizes economic development, reduces stranded-cost risk, and preserves reliability.


Agentic Infrastructure LLC
